items.title: Appendicitis
paragraphs: The appendix is a small finger-shaped pouch attached to the large bowel. When it becomes inflamed or blocked, it causes appendicitis.

Typical signs are tummy pain that starts around the belly button and moves to the lower right side, with loss of appetite, vomiting and fever. Young children may simply seem unwell, unsettled or refuse to walk or jump.
Appendicitis needs prompt assessment because a delay can lead to the appendix bursting. Treatment is usually an operation to remove the appendix (appendicectomy), often done through keyhole surgery.

items.title: Inguinal hernia
paragraphs: An inguinal hernia is a bulge in the groin (sometimes extending into the scrotum or labia) that appears when a child cries, coughs or strains, and may disappear when relaxed. It happens when a small channel that should close before birth stays open, letting bowel push through.
It is common in babies and young children, especially premature babies. A hernia does not heal by itself and is repaired with a short operation, usually as a day case, either open or by keyhole.
Seek urgent care if the bulge becomes hard, painful, discoloured or cannot be gently pushed back, or if your child is vomiting or very unsettled.

items.title: Undescended testis & torsion of the testis
items.popupTitle: Undescended testis & torsion of the testis
paragraphs: Undescended testis: one or both testes are not in the scrotum. Some move down on their own in the first few months of life. If a testis has not descended by about 6 months, your child should be assessed. Treatment is a small operation (orchidopexy) to place the testis in the scrotum, usually advised in the first year or so of life.

Torsion of the testis: the testis twists and cuts off its own blood supply. It causes sudden, severe pain in the scrotum or lower tummy, with swelling and often vomiting, and can affect boys of any age. This is a surgical emergency: go to the nearest emergency department immediately, as the testis can be lost within a few hours.

items.title: Repair of lacerations
paragraphs: A laceration is a cut that is deep, gaping or in a place that needs careful closing. Children often get them from falls, sharp objects or sports.

The wound is cleaned, checked for depth and for any damage to deeper structures, and then closed with stitches, skin glue or adhesive strips. For young or anxious children, or for larger wounds on the face and hands, the repair may be done under sedation or general anaesthesia so it is painless and neat.
Until your child is seen, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth to control bleeding. Repair is best done soon after the injury.

items.title: Burn injuries
paragraphs: Burns in children are most often scalds from hot drinks, water or food. First aid is to cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes, remove clothing and jewellery that is not stuck to the skin, and cover loosely with clean cling film or a non-fluffy cloth. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams.
Please have your child assessed for any burn larger than the size of their palm, or on the face, hands, feet, genitals or over a joint, or if it blisters or looks deep.
Treatment ranges from specialised dressings to, for deeper burns, surgery such as skin grafting, with attention to healing and scarring.

items.title: Hydrocoele
paragraphs: A hydrocoele is a collection of fluid around a testis. It shows as a painless, smooth swelling of the scrotum, often looking bluish or translucent, and is common in newborn boys.

Many hydrocoeles in babies settle on their own by the age of 12 to 18 months. Surgery is considered if the swelling persists, keeps getting bigger, or is linked to a hernia. A doctor will examine your child to tell the two apart.

items.title: Tongue tie
paragraphs: Tongue tie (ankyloglossia) is when the band of tissue under the tongue is short or tight and limits how far the tongue can move.
In some babies it can cause difficulty with latching and breastfeeding; in older children it may affect eating or certain speech sounds. Many children have no problems and need no treatment.
If it is causing problems, a quick procedure to release the band (frenotomy) can be done. Dr. Muniswaran will assess feeding and movement first and advise whether it is needed.

items.title: Lumps and bumps
paragraphs: Lumps and bumps are very common in children, including skin lumps, cysts, enlarged glands (lymph nodes) and swellings on the head, neck, tummy or limbs. Most are harmless.

A lump should still be examined to find out what it is. Please come in sooner if it is growing, hard, painful, red, or comes with fever, tiredness or weight loss. An ultrasound may be arranged, and some lumps are removed with a small operation.

items.title: Tracheo-esophageal fistula
paragraphs: Some babies are born with the food pipe (oesophagus) not fully formed. It often ends in a blind pouch and may be wrongly connected to the windpipe.
Typical signs are drooling or frothy saliva, and coughing, choking or turning blue with the first feeds. It is usually picked up soon after birth.
Treatment is an operation in the first days of life to join the oesophagus and close the abnormal connection. Because other conditions can occur alongside it, your baby will be checked thoroughly.

items.title: Diaphragmatic hernia
paragraphs: The diaphragm is the muscle between the chest and the tummy. In a diaphragmatic hernia there is a hole in it, so organs from the tummy move up into the chest and can limit lung growth.
It is sometimes seen on a pregnancy scan, or shows as breathing difficulty soon after birth. Your baby is stabilised in the newborn intensive care unit first.
Surgery then moves the organs back into the tummy and closes the hole. In selected babies this can be done by keyhole surgery through the chest.

items.title: Duodenal and other intestinal atresia
paragraphs: In intestinal atresia, part of the bowel has not formed fully, leaving a blockage. The duodenum (the first part of the small bowel) is a common site.
Signs include vomiting (often green), a swollen tummy and not passing stools. It may be suspected during pregnancy because of extra fluid around the baby.
Treatment is an operation to bypass or join up the blocked section once your baby is stable. Your baby will also be checked for other related conditions.

items.title: Anorectal malformation
paragraphs: In an anorectal malformation the anus and rectum have not formed normally. The anal opening may be missing, narrow or in the wrong position. It is usually noticed at the first newborn check.
Treatment depends on the type. Some babies need a temporary stoma (a bowel opening on the tummy) first, followed by a reconstruction operation later.
Your baby will also be checked for other conditions, and follow-up continues for years to support bowel control.

items.title: Hirschsprung's disease
paragraphs: In Hirschsprung's disease, nerve cells are missing from a section of the bowel, so it cannot relax and pass stool normally.

A newborn may not pass the first stool within 24 to 48 hours, or may have a swollen tummy and vomiting. In older children it can show as severe, long-standing constipation. Diagnosis uses a contrast enema and a small bowel biopsy.
Treatment is surgery to remove the affected bowel and bring healthy bowel down to the anus (a pull-through), sometimes by keyhole. Seek urgent care for fever, vomiting and a swollen tummy.

items.title: Malrotation
paragraphs: In malrotation the bowel did not settle into its normal position during development. It can twist (volvulus) and cut off its own blood supply.
The warning sign is sudden green (bile-stained) vomiting, often with a swollen or painful tummy, usually in a baby. This is an emergency and needs immediate medical attention.
Treatment is an operation to untwist the bowel and place it in a safe position.

items.title: Pyloric stenosis
paragraphs: The pylorus is the muscle at the outlet of the stomach. In pyloric stenosis it thickens and blocks milk from leaving the stomach. It usually appears between 2 and 8 weeks of age, and is more common in first-born boys.
The typical sign is forceful, projectile vomiting after feeds, with the baby still hungry afterwards and not gaining weight well. An ultrasound confirms it.
After any dehydration is corrected, a short operation (pyloromyotomy), done open or by keyhole, relieves the blockage. Most babies feed again within hours and recover very well.

items.title: Congenital abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis / omphalocele)
paragraphs: Gastroschisis: bowel sits outside the tummy, through a small hole beside the belly button, with no covering.
Omphalocele: organs sit outside the tummy in a thin sac at the belly button, and other conditions may be present.

Both are usually seen on pregnancy scans, so delivery can be planned at a hospital with newborn surgical care. The organs are protected and returned to the tummy, either in one operation or gradually over several days, and the abdominal wall is then closed. Feeding can take time to build up.

sections.title: Paediatric Urology
sections.subtitle: Disorders of the urinary tract and genitalia

items.title: Disorders of the kidneys
paragraphs: These include kidney cysts, infections such as a kidney abscess, and hydronephrosis (a swollen kidney because urine is not draining well). Many are first seen on a pregnancy scan.
Children may have fever, tummy or flank pain, repeated urine infections, or blood in the urine. Ultrasound and other scans show what is happening.
Treatment ranges from watching and antibiotics to drainage or an operation, depending on the cause and how the kidney is working.
items.desc: Cysts and tumours of the kidney, infections such as renal abscess, hydronephrosis, etc.

items.title: Disorders of the ureter
paragraphs: The ureter is the tube carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder. Problems include a blockage where it leaves the kidney (pelviureteric junction obstruction), a blockage where it enters the bladder (vesicoureteric junction obstruction), and vesicoureteral reflux, where urine flows back up towards the kidney.
They can cause kidney swelling and urine infections, and may affect kidney growth. Tests include ultrasound, kidney scans and a bladder X-ray study.
Many children only need monitoring and preventive antibiotics. Others need surgery to relieve the blockage or to correct the reflux.
items.desc: Pelviureteric junction obstruction, vesicoureteric junction obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, etc.

items.title: Disorders of the bladder
paragraphs: Neurogenic bladder: the nerves controlling the bladder do not work normally, for example in spina bifida. Bladder exstrophy: a rare condition in which the bladder forms open on the outside of the lower tummy and needs staged reconstruction.
The aims of care are to protect the kidneys, prevent infection and achieve dryness where possible. Treatment can include medicines, regular catheter drainage and surgery.
Long-term follow-up is an important part of the care.

items.title: Disorders of the urethra
paragraphs: Phimosis: a tight foreskin that cannot be pulled back. This is normal in young children and often settles; treatment is considered if it causes infections or scarring.
Posterior urethral valve: a membrane in a boy's urethra that blocks urine flow, needing early treatment.

Hypospadias and epispadias: the urine opening is on the underside (hypospadias) or top (epispadias) of the penis rather than the tip. Repair is by surgery, usually planned in the first couple of years of life. A boy with hypospadias should be assessed before any circumcision.
items.desc: Phimosis, posterior urethral valve, hypospadias, epispadias, etc.

items.title: Disorders of the genitalia
paragraphs: Undescended testis: a testis that has not moved down into the scrotum; a small operation (orchidopexy) places it correctly.
Intersex conditions (differences of sex development): these need careful, sensitive assessment by a specialist team, with parents involved at every step and no rush to decide.
Imperforate hymen: a thin membrane blocks the vaginal opening. It can be noticed in a newborn or later in puberty with pain and absent periods. A simple minor procedure opens it.
items.desc: Undescended testis, intersex conditions, imperforate hymen.

items.title: Tumours of the kidney
paragraphs: Wilms' tumour is the most common kidney cancer in children and usually occurs under the age of 5. It often shows as a painless lump or swelling in the tummy, and sometimes blood in the urine, fever or raised blood pressure.

Scans and tests confirm the diagnosis. Treatment is planned with a children's cancer team and usually combines chemotherapy and surgery to remove the affected kidney, sometimes with radiotherapy. Most children do well with treatment.

items.title: Laparoscopic orchidopexy
paragraphs: Keyhole surgery to find an undescended testis and bring it down into the scrotum. It is especially helpful when the testis cannot be felt, because the surgeon can look inside the tummy with a small camera.
It is done through very small cuts and is usually a day-case operation.

items.title: Laparoscopic appendicectomy
paragraphs: Removal of the appendix through a few small cuts, using a camera and fine instruments, to treat appendicitis.
Compared with open surgery it usually means smaller scars, less pain and a quicker return to normal activity.

items.title: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
paragraphs: Keyhole removal of the gallbladder, needed when gallstones or gallbladder disease cause pain, vomiting or jaundice. These problems can occur in children, sometimes alongside certain blood conditions.
Most children go home within a day or two and recover quickly. The gallbladder is not essential for normal digestion.

items.title: Thoracoscopic repair of diaphragmatic hernia
paragraphs: A keyhole operation done through the chest (thoracoscopy) to close the hole in the diaphragm and return the organs to the tummy.
It is suitable for selected babies who are stable enough, and can mean smaller scars and less strain on the chest wall as the child grows.

items.title: Laparoscopic hernia repair
paragraphs: The hernia opening is closed using small keyhole cuts. The surgeon can also look at the other side at the same time.
It is usually done as a day case, with small scars and a quick recovery.

items.title: Laparoscopic ovarian surgery
paragraphs: Keyhole surgery for ovarian cysts, a twisted ovary (torsion) or ovarian growths. The aim is to protect healthy ovarian tissue and future fertility wherever possible.
A twisted ovary causes sudden, severe lower tummy pain, often with vomiting, and is an emergency that needs immediate medical attention.

items.title: Laparoscopic Hirschsprung's pull-through surgery
paragraphs: For Hirschsprung's disease, the affected bowel is freed and removed using keyhole techniques and the healthy bowel is joined to the anus.
Keyhole methods mean smaller cuts and often a quicker return to feeding and normal activity.

items.title: Ovarian pathology
paragraphs: This covers ovarian cysts, a twisted ovary (torsion) and ovarian growths. Signs can include lower tummy pain, swelling and vomiting, and an ultrasound is usually the first test.
Most cysts are harmless and settle by themselves. Surgery is advised if a cyst is large, keeps growing, is twisted or looks suspicious, and the aim is always to preserve healthy ovarian tissue.

items.title: Congenital anomalies
paragraphs: Some girls are born with differences in how the vagina, uterus or nearby structures formed, such as a blocked vaginal opening or a dividing wall. These may be noticed at birth, or later in puberty with pain or absent periods.
Scans help to plan care. Treatment is tailored to each girl, from a minor procedure to reconstruction, and is often timed with growth and puberty.

items.title: Labial adhesions
paragraphs: Labial adhesions happen when the inner lips of the vulva stick together. They are common in girls from infancy to about 6 years of age and often cause no symptoms.
Sometimes they cause urine to collect or dribble, or irritation. Many settle on their own or with a prescribed cream. Please do not try to separate them at home. Surgery is rarely needed.
